title: Former Corsicana Councilmember Sues City, Alleging Retaliation That Drove Him From Office
sub: Lawsuit says officials stonewalled Will Jones's records requests and backed a demand for his private phone the day he proposed a countywide task force.
body: Will Jones joined the Corsicana City Council in May 2024, two months after his brother, Deantae Parks, was killed in Corsicana. Over the next year he asked questions: as a brother, about the investigation into the killing, and as a councilmember, about City spending and public safety. A federal lawsuit filed by GFA LAW, PLLC alleges that City leaders answered those questions with retaliation that ultimately drove him from office.

According to the complaint, Mr. Jones's requests for records about his brother's case and about local gun violence were delayed, restarted, and answered only in part, even after the Texas Attorney General ruled in March 2025 that the homicide records had to be released with redactions. Another councilmember, the complaint says, received comparable records promptly. The complaint also alleges that an email from one of Mr. Jones's constituents was used against him at a public council meeting, and that police personnel were told not to cooperate with him.

Then came the demand for his phone. On May 29, 2025, the same day Mr. Jones proposed a countywide law-enforcement task force, the Texas Municipal Police Association filed a public-information request for communications on his privately owned phone. The complaint alleges that City officials helped move that request forward. The phone held family messages, business records, and conversations with lawyers, including communications about his brother's case. The request was withdrawn four days after Mr. Jones resigned, and three weeks later the Attorney General determined that the material was not public information at all.
The complaint alleges that the mounting pressure took a serious toll on Mr. Jones's health, and that he stepped down in July 2025 on the advice of his medical provider.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Dallas, names the City of Corsicana, former Mayor Michael Fletcher, City Attorney Kerri Anderson Donica, City Manager James Holgersson, and former Police Chief Robert Johnson. It asks a jury to decide whether Mr. Jones's constitutional rights were violated and to award damages. The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

body.q: Speaking up and asking for records is how citizens hold their government accountable. The First Amendment protects Will Jones's right to do both, and this lawsuit asks a federal court to enforce it.

summary: Will Jones joined the Corsicana City Council in May 2024, two months after his brother, Deantae Parks, was killed in Corsicana. A federal lawsuit filed by GFA LAW, PLLC alleges that City leaders answered his questions with retaliation that ultimately drove him from office.

title: GFA LAW Files Whistleblower Suit Against City of Trinidad Over Firing of Its Former City Administrator
sub: Lawsuit alleges Lindsey Patterson was suspended within hours, and fired within a week, of reporting the mishandling of public funds.
body: TEMPLE, Texas. GFA LAW, PLLC has filed suit on behalf of Lindsey Patterson, the former City Administrator and City Secretary of the City of Trinidad, in the District Court of Henderson County, Texas. The lawsuit, brought under the Texas Whistleblower Act, alleges that the City suspended and then terminated Ms. Patterson in retaliation for reporting the mishandling of public money.

According to the petition, on February 20, 2026, Ms. Patterson reported to the City's Chief of Police that Event Committee funds were being held outside the City's official depository, contrary to Texas law governing the safekeeping of public funds. The lawsuit alleges that within roughly eight hours of that report the City placed her on administrative leave, and that one week later, on February 27, 2026, it terminated her employment. The City then named Cynthia Sam Dosier as City Administrator in her place.

The petition seeks reinstatement or front pay, lost wages and benefits, compensatory damages, court costs, and attorney's fees. The case, Lindsey Patterson v. City of Trinidad, Texas, was filed on July 9, 2026, and a cause number will be assigned by the Henderson County District Clerk. The City has not yet filed a response, and the allegations in the petition have not been tested in court.

GFA LAW contends that the firing of Ms. Patterson, and the naming of her replacement, marked the beginning of the current City Council's pattern of retaliation against those who question how Trinidad is run. Ms. Patterson is the fifth GFA LAW client to bring suit against the City of Trinidad, and the firm expects additional cases to follow.

body.q: This began when Trinidad's leaders fired a public servant for telling the truth about the public's money. Our goal is simple: to put the power in Trinidad back in the hands of its residents, and to hold accountable a City Council we believe has corrupted the public's trust.

title: GFA LAW Statement: An Update in Bivens v. City of Trinidad
sub: The Council wanted a sitting judge gone, knew it needed cause, and removed her without due process for doing her job.
body: TEMPLE, Texas. GFA LAW, PLLC has filed an amended petition in its lawsuit against the City of Trinidad on behalf of Municipal Judge Shellena Bivens.

As we have said from the start, the story here is simple. The Council wanted Judge Bivens gone. It knew that a sitting municipal judge holds a fixed term and cannot be removed without cause, so it went looking for a reason. The one it chose was that Judge Bivens had done her job and ruled on a case before her, a reason that one of the Council's own members admitted, under oath, she could not even say was misconduct under the law. The Council then removed Judge Bivens with no notice, no charges, and no hearing. The petition alleges that this denied her due process and violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments and the Texas Open Meetings Act.

Judge Bivens is seeking all available remedies, including punitive damages against the responsible officials. A judge who can be removed for how she rules is no protection to anyone who comes before her court. The people of Trinidad deserve better, and we intend to prove this case in court.
summary: TEMPLE, Texas. GFA LAW, PLLC has filed an amended petition in its lawsuit against the City of Trinidad on behalf of Municipal Judge Shellena Bivens.

title: Fort Worth Police Department Violates Citizen's Rights at Pride Festival
sub: GFA LAW Announces Representation of David Grisham; Vows to Fight Citation
body: GFA LAW, PLLC announced today that it is representing David Grisham, a street preacher who was threatened with arrest and subsequently cited by officers of the Fort Worth Police Department for engaging in peaceful and protected speech outside the Trinity Pride Festival. GFA LAW intends to vigorously challenge the citation and any related enforcement action as a direct and unlawful violation. Mr. Grisham was exercising his right to express his views on matters of significant public concern. The Fort Worth Police Department responded, not by protecting his constitutional rights, but by threatening him with arrest and ultimately issuing a citation. That citation is indefensible. The Noise Ordinance clearly requires that officers must first measure the challenged noise using a decibel meter. See Ordinance Section 23-8 attached. This ordinance was not followed because no officer performed a decibel check. Officers failed to follow the Fort Worth Ordinance. Moreover, the ordinance violates state preemption. Tex. Penal code 1.08, to wit: Sec. 1.08. PREEMPTION. “No governmental subdivision or agency may enact or enforce a law that makes any conduct covered by this code an offense subject to a criminal penalty. This section shall apply only as long as the law governing the conduct proscribed by this code is legally enforceable.” Texas already has an “unreasonable noise” regulation, so Fort Worth's Ordinance is preempted when it contradicts Texas law. Tex. Penal Code 42.01(a)(5) makes it an offense if a person “makes unreasonable noise in a public place other than a sport shooting range.” Tex. Penal Code 42.01(c)(2) defines unreasonable noise: “a noise is presumed to be unreasonable if the noise exceeds a decibel level of 85 after the person making the noise receives notice from a magistrate or peace officer that the noise is a public nuisance.” Because Fort Worth's Ordinance lowers the limit to 80 decibels, it is unlawful ab initio. GFA LAW calls on the City of Fort Worth to immediately dismiss the citation and retract any related enforcement action. CJ Grisham, Senior Partner
Note: David Grisham is an Amarillo-based street preacher and evangelist. He shares no known familial or professional relationship with CJ Grisham, Senior Partner of GFA LAW, PLLC.

title: Judge Confirms Trinidad Officers Withheld Key Facts From Court to Target Political Critic
sub: GFA LAW Client Jennifer Combs Was Innocent from Day One, Says Attorney
body: In a letter dated June 8, 2026, Henderson County 392nd District Court Judge R. Scott McKee confirmed what GFA LAW has argued from the start: Sergeant Robert McCumsey and Investigator Cameron Beckham withheld critical facts from the court when they sought a warrant to prosecute Jennifer Combs over a Facebook post about Trinidad's water supply. The officers knew about citizen complaints, water quality concerns, and the full context of Mrs. Combs' statements. They disclosed none of it. Instead, they presented a stripped-down affidavit designed to manufacture probable cause for a politically motivated prosecution.

Mrs. Combs was arrested and charged with a felony for speaking publicly about her community's drinking water. A Henderson County grand jury refused to indict her in May 2026. Now a district judge has confirmed the warrant that launched that prosecution was built on an incomplete and misleading affidavit.

body.q: “Jennifer Combs did nothing wrong. She spoke up about a public health issue and was punished for it by officers who used the courts as a weapon. The judge saw through it. Now a federal jury will too.”

body: Judge McKee has ordered that any future warrant from either officer will require a personal appearance under oath. That is an extraordinary sanction, and it reflects exactly how seriously the court views this misconduct.

GFA LAW has filed suit on behalf of Mrs. Combs in the Eastern District of Texas against the officers and the City of Trinidad under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging First Amendment retaliation and malicious prosecution. Combs v. Gregory et al., No. 6:26-cv-235, is ongoing. Judge McKee is to be commended for refusing to allow his court to be used as an instrument of political punishment.

title: GFA LAW Statement: On the Conduct of Supporters
sub: GFA LAW Calls for Focus on the Law; Rejects Harassment, Threats, and Retaliation Against Individuals
body: GFA LAW, PLLC is aware that individuals who support our clients and their causes have, in some instances, directed threatening, harassing, or otherwise inappropriate conduct toward city employees, law enforcement officers, and other individuals connected to our ongoing litigation. We are issuing this statement to be unambiguous: GFA LAW does not support, endorse, or condone any of it.

We want to be clear about what we mean. If you are threatening someone's job, their family, their safety, or their peace of mind — stop. If you are flooding someone's personal phone or email with harassment — stop. If you are showing up at someone's home or workplace to intimidate them — stop. None of that is advocacy. None of that is justice. And none of it helps our clients.

The legal battle in Trinidad, Texas is a battle about accountability, about the rule of law, and about the rights of the people we represent. That battle is won in courtrooms, through evidence, and through the legal process. It is not won by making individual employees fear for their livelihoods or their safety. Many of the people who work for these institutions are not the decision-makers whose conduct is at issue. They are working people doing their jobs. They are not our targets, and they should not be yours.

GFA LAW actively rejects the use of harassment, intimidation, or extralegal pressure as tools in service of our clients' causes. Anyone engaging in this conduct is not acting on our behalf, is not helping our clients, and is potentially harming the very cases they claim to support.

If you believe in what our clients are fighting for, the best thing you can do is stay focused on the city's conduct — not on complicating these matters by introducing behavior that undermines the legitimacy of their claims. Support our clients. Follow the proceedings. Share the facts. Let the law do what it is designed to do.

title: A Note to Those Who Have Reached Out to GFA LAW
sub: On Response Times, Firm Capacity, and Our Commitment to the Clients We Serve
body: GFA LAW, PLLC is a two-attorney firm. We handle civil rights, constitutional defense, Second Amendment restoration, and criminal defense. We are grateful for the trust so many Texans have placed in us. That trust is also, candidly, the reason for this statement.

Our firm currently carries more than 250 active intake submissions. We have two attorneys. Our first obligation is to the clients we have already taken on: people who have hired us, trusted us, and are counting on us to show up. We will not compromise their representation by overextending.

If you have contacted GFA LAW and have not received a response, please know this: our silence is not a judgment on your case. It is not a signal that your situation lacks merit or that your rights were not violated. We simply cannot take on more than we can serve well.

Our initial consultation fee is currently set at $350. We are transparent about why: it is not a revenue mechanism. It is how we ensure that the consultations we do conduct go to people who are serious about their matter and who understand that our time is genuinely limited at this stage of the firm's growth.

We hope to grow. We are working toward a day when GFA LAW can serve a far larger caseload and give every person who contacts us the attention their situation deserves. To those already represented: you are our priority. To those still waiting: thank you for your patience and your understanding.

title: Journalist Jennifer Combs Unlawfully Charged for Reporting on Public Water Safety Concerns
sub: Trinidad Police Chief's Misuse of Texas Penal Code § 42.06 Constitutes a Direct Assault on First Amendment Rights and a Retaliatory Attack on a Persistent Critic of City Officials
body: NAVARRO COUNTY, TEXAS — Mrs. Jennifer Combs, a working journalist and resident of Navarro County, has been criminally charged by City of Trinidad Police Chief Charles Gregory for the act of informing her community about reports she received concerning the safety of the local public water supply. The charge, brought under Texas Penal Code § 42.06 for allegedly communicating a false report, represents an extraordinary overreach of governmental authority, a direct violation of rights guaranteed by the First Amendment to the United States Constitution, and unmistakable retaliation against a journalist who has long been a vocal critic of high-ranking officials within the City of Trinidad.

Mrs. Combs is well known throughout the region for her reporting on matters of public concern. Her work consistently addresses issues that the citizens of Navarro County and surrounding areas have a clear and compelling interest in understanding. The Facebook post that gave rise to these charges did precisely what responsible journalism is supposed to do: it informed the public of credible reports she had received from members of the community regarding the quality of their drinking water, including allegations that at least one individual has been hospitalized as a result of consuming that water.

Communicating with the public about a potentially contaminated water supply is not a crime. It is the very kind of speech that the Founders sought to protect when they wrote the First Amendment. The United States Supreme Court has affirmed time and again that speech on matters of public concern occupies the highest rung of the hierarchy of First Amendment values. Reports about the safety of a municipal water system fall squarely within that protection.

Texas Penal Code § 42.06 was enacted to address the narrow circumstance of an individual who knowingly initiates a false emergency — such as falsely reporting a fire, bombing, or other incident requiring an immediate emergency response. At no point did Mrs. Combs create, or attempt to create, any such emergency. She summoned no responders. She triggered no evacuations. She did nothing more than share with her readers the very reports that local officials should themselves be transparently addressing. The statute simply does not apply to her conduct, and any prosecutor acting in good faith would recognize as much.

Make no mistake: the charge filed against Mrs. Combs is a transparent abuse of authority. When a public official wields the machinery of the criminal justice system to silence a journalist who is asking uncomfortable questions about public safety, that official is no longer enforcing the law — he is weaponizing it. Such conduct chills not only Mrs. Combs’ speech, but the speech of every citizen, journalist, and whistleblower who might otherwise come forward with information the public deserves to know.

The context surrounding these charges makes their retaliatory nature unmistakable. Mrs. Combs is a well-known and persistent critic of several high-ranking officials within the City of Trinidad. For years, she has used her platform to scrutinize their conduct, question their decisions, and hold them publicly accountable on matters ranging from governance to public safety. The decision to invoke the criminal code against her — over a Facebook post about the community’s drinking water, no less — did not arise in a vacuum. It is the latest, and most alarming, chapter in a documented pattern of hostility from City officials toward a journalist whose reporting they have long resented.

These charges are nothing more than political retaliation dressed up in the language of law enforcement. They are precisely the type of viewpoint-based government action that the First Amendment was designed to prevent. The Constitution does not permit public officials to prosecute their critics into silence, and the courts have repeatedly recognized that retaliatory prosecutions of this kind expose the officials involved to serious personal and constitutional liability.

We intend to vigorously defend Mrs. Combs against these baseless charges. We will pursue every available legal remedy, including but not limited to dismissal of the charges, civil action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for the deprivation of constitutional rights under color of law, and any and all other relief to which Mrs. Combs and the public are entitled. Those who would weaponize the criminal code to punish protected speech and silence political opposition should expect to be held fully accountable.

Mrs. Combs will not be intimidated into silence, and neither will the community she serves. The residents of Navarro County deserve answers about the quality of their water — not the arrest of the messenger who dared to ask the questions on their behalf.
